description: pkey-peer/1 byte-level rules (WIRE-CONTRACT-V5 sections 15.4 to 15.7 and 15.9; plans/CC-01-cloud-connect.md 2.4, 2.6, 2.7, 2.9). Hex fields are lower-case. `adverts`: `names` (the mode-a instance: p1- and the first 16 characters of the lower-case RFC 4648 base32, no padding, of HMAC-SHA256(K_disc, 'pkey-peer/1 disc' || 0x00 || u64be(epoch) || the 24 device-id bytes)), `epochs` (now / 900), `tags` (the h value), `txt` (TXT parsing), `instances` (the name shape) and `browse` (which roster device an instance belongs to); `prologue`; `psk`; `sas` (the code with its commit and reveal rows); `frames` (TCP framing); `records` (flags, MORE, the critical and mode rules, the 1 MiB limit); `relayEnvelopes`; `handshakePayloads`; `lanAddresses` (which peer addresses a device dials or accepts, and the per-address count key); `mdnsAnswers` (which A and AAAA records a browser believes). A device id is 32 base64url characters and is hashed and sent as its 24 decoded bytes. The device proof is device-proof.json. Append-only: a new row keeps peerMatrixVersion; a changed row or rule bumps it.

sas.note: h is the 32-byte Noise handshake hash. code = u32be(HKDF-SHA256(salt = h, ikm = nD || nM, info = 'pkey-peer/1 sas' || 0x00 || mode)[0..4]) mod 10^6, shown as six digits with leading zeros and a space between the triples. A nonce and a commitment travel as 43 base64url characters; the body of SAS_COMMIT is the compact JSON object with the member c, SAS_NONCE nM and SAS_REVEAL nD. c = SHA-256(nD).

frames.note: A frame is u16be len || Noise message, len 1..65535. `decode` reads a byte stream: it returns the complete frames and the unread rest; a zero length closes the session with peer_bad_frame, wherever it occurs.

records.note: A Noise transport plaintext is u16be type || u8 flags || body. Flag bit 0 is MORE; any other bit closes with peer_bad_frame. A body is {fill, count} (one hex byte repeated) where it is large. `types` is the type table; a type outside it is unknown, critical when bit 0x8000 is set. In `sessions` each record is read in order and `at` is the 0-based index of the record that closed the session. Checks run per record: flags, then a continuation of another type (peer_bad_frame), then the type (unknown critical, mode), then the running size over 1 MiB (peer_bad_frame), then, on the last record of a chain, a fixed body length (peer_bad_frame). An unknown non-critical type is dropped, MORE chain and all. delivered lists the reassembled messages as type, length and SHA-256.

relayEnvelopes.note: One binary WebSocket message is an envelope: op byte, then the layout of 15.7. A device is its 24 decoded device-id bytes. MEMBERS carries the count n as one byte; PONG echoes the 8 bytes of the PING it answers. `dir` is the sender: toRoom (a client to the room) or toClient. `messages` encode and decode both ways; `refused` rows decode to nothing; `sizes` rows are an op, a 24-byte device, a session and a run of `fill` bytes up to `total` bytes, whole. A message over 65,564 bytes is refused.

handshakePayloads.note: Handshake payloads (15.5): strict JSON of 15.1/1.2, an object, at most 8 KiB of UTF-8. Message 1 needs v = 1 and no cert; messages 2 and 3 need v = 1 and caps (at most 32 entries matching ^[a-z0-9]+/[0-9]+$). Mode a adds cert (a non-empty string; its verification is cases.json peerCertCases) and ring (an integer from 1 to 2^53 - 1); modes v and p refuse a cert. Unknown members are ignored. `payload` is the text, `payloadHex` the raw bytes where the text is not valid UTF-8, `payloadPad` the text prefix + count x fill + suffix. `want.caps` is the list as sent; the session uses `intersection`: the entries both lists hold, once each, in byte order.

lanAddresses.note: LAN addresses (15.4.1): lanVerdict(remote, local, allowLoopback) -> {dial, key}, applied to an accepted socket before it takes a slot or is read, to a dialled address's text before connect and again to the connected socket before its first byte. `remote` is the socket's peer address as text and `local` its own address (absent: unknown). Spelling: a zone is `%` and 1 to 15 characters of U+0021 to U+007E other than `%`; an empty or longer zone, a second `%`, a control, a space or a non-ASCII character, a zone on IPv4 and a zone on an IPv4-mapped address are malformed and refused; the grammar is strict (RFC 3986 IPv4address and IPv6address): no whitespace, NUL, port, prefix length, trailing dot, brackets, non-ASCII digits or leading-zero octet. IPv4-mapped (::ffff:0:0/96) is judged as its IPv4 address. IPv4: 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, and 127/8 only with allowLoopback. IPv6: fe80::/10; fc00::/7, which with a known `local` must be IPv6 (not mapped) in the same /64; ::1 only with allowLoopback; an address in 2000::/3, outside 2001::/32 (Teredo) and 2002::/16 (6to4), only when `local` is IPv6 (not mapped) in the same /64. Anything else, and text that is not an address, is refused. `key` is the per-address connection count key: dotted IPv4, or RFC 5952 lower-case IPv6 text without its zone, except that a link-local (fe80::/10) key keeps its zone; null when `dial` is false. `group` is the per-/64 count key of an IPv6 key (`<masked address>/64`, with `%zone` appended for link-local), null for IPv4 and for no key. `candidates` holds the rule for a CANDIDATES entry (15.6).

candidates.note: CANDIDATES entries (15.6, 15.4.1): candidateTarget(entry, interfaces) -> {host, port} or null. `interfaces` lists the device's own addresses, one per entry: `{address, prefix, up, tunnel}`, `tunnel` meaning a VPN, tunnel, point-to-point or pseudo-interface. An entry is dialled only when all hold: it is `a.b.c.d:port` or `[addr]:port` (brackets only around IPv6) with a plain decimal port from 1024 to 65535 (no sign, no leading zero, no space, no other character); an IPv6 address is in RFC 5952 text, has no zone, is not IPv4-mapped and is not in fe80::/10; the address is not one of the device's own; it lies inside the subnet (address and prefix) of an up, non-tunnel interface address; and lanVerdict(address, that interface address, false) allows it. `target.host` is the address as dialled.

mdnsAnswers.note: mDNS address learning (15.4 Addresses). `packet` is one mDNS response as lower-case hex (header, then the answer and additional sections; names may be compressed, RFC 1035 4.1.4). `source` is the packet's source address as text and `zone` the interface it arrived on (null: none). A browser believes an A or AAAA record only when its address equals `source` (so an A record is never believed in an IPv6 packet, nor an AAAA in an IPv4 packet); the section a record sits in does not matter. A link-local (fe80::/10) address is learned as `<RFC 5952 text>%<zone>`; any other address has no zone. A name keeps at most 4 addresses, of any family, in first-seen order, and a repeat is not a second address. Only address records teach addresses: a PTR goodbye (TTL 0) teaches none and does not remove any, and no row pins the TTL of an address record. `prior` (absent: nothing held) is the table the browser held before the packet, in first-seen order; `learned` is the table after it: the `{name, address}` entries in first-seen order. Names are lower case. Rows need an own DNS codec: Node, Python, Kotlin JVM and Godot GDScript run them; Swift and Android leave address learning to the OS resolver.
